## The question

A language model has read an enormous amount of finance. Working papers, textbooks,
factor zoo surveys, decades of published anomalies. So here is a question worth
asking directly:

> Can you *farm* tradable equity signals out of that knowledge?

Not "can it explain momentum" — obviously it can. The question is whether it can
propose a **new** cross-sectional predictor, one that survives a ruthless backtest
it was not allowed to influence.

The honest way to answer that is to build the ruthless backtest first, and only
then let the model start guessing. That inversion is the whole project. It is easy
to build a pipeline where the model proposes ideas and you eyeball the Sharpe
ratios and get excited. It is harder, and much more useful, to build one where the
model's ideas are judged by machinery that cannot be talked into anything.

This post is about that machinery: what it does, why each piece is there, and how
you would write a signal for it yourself.

## What "farming" means here

The setup is a division of labour between three agents and one harness.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f3460', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'primaryBorderColor': '#e94560', 'lineColor': '#a0a8c0', 'secondaryColor': '#1a1a2e', 'tertiaryColor': '#16213e', 'clusterBkg': '#16213e', 'clusterBorder': '#e94560', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#1a1a2e', 'fontFamily': 'inherit'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    FRONTIER[("Research frontier\nwhat the library holds\nwhich themes are thin")]

    subgraph AGENTS["The creative half — costs money, can be wrong"]
        IDEA["Idea agent · Opus 5\nhypothesis + mechanism\nformula, sign, references"]
        DATA["Data agent · Sonnet 5\nmap concepts to real columns\ngate on coverage"]
        CODER["Coder agent · Sonnet 5\nwrite the Signal module\nself-correct on failure"]
        IDEA --> DATA --> CODER
    end

    subgraph HARNESS["The judging half — deterministic, identical for everyone"]
        VAL["No-look-ahead validator"]
        BT["Decile long/short backtest"]
        ROB["Robustness battery"]
        STAT["Factor attribution\nDeflated Sharpe · BH-FDR"]
        VAL --> BT --> ROB --> STAT
    end

    LEDGER[("Ledger\nevery attempt, including\nthe ones that died")]

    FRONTIER --> IDEA
    CODER --> VAL
    STAT --> LEDGER
    LEDGER -.->|raises the bar| STAT
    STAT --> ARTICLE["Published results"]
```

The **idea agent** runs on the most capable model available, because generating a
genuinely novel economic hypothesis is the one step where capability plausibly
matters. It gets a research frontier — what is already in the library, which
categories and data sources are thin — and is told to go somewhere new.

The **data agent** runs on a cheaper model and does something unglamorous but
essential: map each requested concept onto a column that actually exists, and kill
the idea if it doesn't. On the first live run this gate caught the idea agent
inventing a column called `macro_cpi_chg12m_scale` out of thin air. No such column.
The hypothesis died before a line of code was written, at a cost of about two cents.

The **coder agent** writes the actual module, then self-corrects against the
validator's complaints for up to three attempts. Its output is treated as
untrusted: a static check rejects file, network and process access before the
module is ever imported.

Then everything hits the same harness. That part has no model in it at all.

## What a signal actually is

This is the concept everything else rests on, and it is simpler than it sounds.

A **cross-sectional signal** is one number per stock per month. That's it. Not a
buy/sell decision, not a price target — just a score.

The crucial property: **only the ranking matters.** The absolute level is
meaningless. A signal that outputs book-to-market ratios between 0.1 and 8, and a
signal that outputs their logarithms, are the same signal. All the harness ever
does with your number is sort by it.

Each month, mechanically:

1. Take every eligible stock — liquid, above $5, common stock, real exchange.
2. Compute the score for each one.
3. Sort. Long the top 10%, short the bottom 10%, equal-weighted.
4. Hold for one month. Earn the spread.
5. Repeat, 280 times, from 2000 to 2024.

If the ranking carries information about next month's returns, the spread is
positive on average and compounds. If it doesn't, you get a random walk with
transaction costs bolted on. That's the entire test.

### Orientation, and why the interface has an `expected_sign`

There's a design wrinkle worth explaining because it shapes how you write a signal.

Some predictors work the "right" way up: high gross profitability predicts high
returns. Others are inverted: high asset growth predicts *low* returns, and so does
high volatility. If every signal had to be written so that "high = good", you'd be
constantly writing `-volatility` or `1/asset_growth`, and guarding the division,
and getting the sign wrong at 2am.

So the interface separates the two concerns. You write the **natural** formula, and
declare which way it points:

```python
class LowVolatility(BaseSignal):
    name = "low_volatility"
    category = "low_risk"
    expected_sign = -1        # LOW vol predicts HIGH return
    description = "Low-volatility anomaly: trailing 1y realized vol (low = long)."

    def compute(self, panel):
        return panel["vol_252"]      # the natural quantity, not its negation
```

The harness multiplies by `expected_sign` before ranking, so after orientation
"high score = go long" always holds. You get to write `vol_252` and mean it.

There is a second archetype too. A `strategy_type = "macro_timing"` signal returns
one number *per date* rather than per stock — a desired market exposure. The
harness standardizes it using only past data, maps it to a position in [−1, 1], and
earns that fraction of the market. Same interface, different shape.

### A worked example: one month, one signal

The description above is abstract enough that it is worth watching a single month
go through the machine. Take `inventory_growth_gap`, one of the farmed signals.
The hypothesis: if a company's warehouse is filling up faster than its sales are
growing, it over-forecast demand, and write-downs and discounts are coming. The
formula is a gap between two growth rates:

```python
inv_g   = inventory / inventory_12mo_ago - 1
sales_g = revenue   / revenue_12mo_ago   - 1
raw     = inv_g - sales_g
```

`expected_sign = -1`, because it is the *large* gap that is the bad case.

Now one month-end. Twenty eligible names, which is small enough to print — the
real cross-section runs 1,500 to 3,000 — sorted by the oriented score:

| Ticker | `raw` (inv − sales growth) | oriented alpha | decile | weight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| TTT | −0.55 | 0.55 | 9 | **+0.50** |
| SSS | −0.31 | 0.31 | 9 | **+0.50** |
| RRR | −0.24 | 0.24 | 8 | 0 |
| QQQ | −0.19 | 0.19 | 8 | 0 |
| … | … | … | … | 0 |
| DDD | 0.25 | −0.25 | 1 | 0 |
| CCC | 0.33 | −0.33 | 1 | 0 |
| BBB | 0.41 | −0.41 | 0 | **−0.50** |
| AAA | 0.62 | −0.62 | 0 | **−0.50** |

Four things happened in that table, and they are the entire trading rule.

**Orientation flipped the sign.** AAA has the worst inventory bloat — stock piling
up 62 percentage points faster than sales — and the multiplication by
`expected_sign = -1` sends it to the bottom of the sort. TTT, running the leanest
inventory, goes to the top. After this step the harness never has to know what the
signal measures; it only knows that high means long.

**The sort became buckets.** Ranks are converted to deciles, using *average* ranks
so that tied scores stay together. Ranking by first-occurrence instead would have
broken ties by the panel's ticker order, i.e. alphabetically, which is a genuinely
strange thing to trade on. The scores are also winsorized at 1% first — that clips
outlier *values* so a company whose inventory tripled cannot distort anything
downstream, while leaving its rank, and therefore its decile, untouched.

**Buckets became weights.** Equal weight within each leg: two longs at +50%, two
shorts at −50%. In the real cross-section that is roughly 200 names a side at
±0.5% each. The book is 100% long and 100% short — dollar neutral, though nothing
here forces the two legs to have matching market exposure. The middle eight
deciles, 80% of the market, are simply not traded.

**Weights met next month's returns.** Say the two longs return +3% and +6% and the
two shorts return −4% and +1%. The long leg earns the average, +4.5%. The bottom
decile's own return averages −1.5%, and since it was held short, subtracting it
adds to the spread: **+6.0% gross** for the month. Then turnover is charged. If the
entire book had to be rebuilt from scratch, the traded notional is 2.0 and the cost
at 10 bps is 20 bps for that month — which is why a slow, fundamentals-driven
signal like this one and a fast monthly-reversal signal are not remotely competing
on equal terms.

Repeat 280 times and that stream of monthly numbers is what every statistic in the
rest of this post is computed from.

## The part that matters: point-in-time correctness

Every backtest is a claim about what you *would have known* at the time. Almost all
the ways to get that wrong are subtle.

**Fundamentals join on the filing date, never the fiscal period.** A company's Q3
figures describe September but become public in November. Joining on the fiscal
date hands your backtest two months of clairvoyance and produces beautiful,
worthless results.

**The universe keeps delisted names.** This one bites in a way that's easy to miss.
When a company is acquired or goes bankrupt it stops appearing in the data — so its
final month has no "next month" to compute a return from, and the naive fix is to
drop the row. But dropping it silently removes the worst outcomes from whichever
decile was holding them. In this dataset, 12,754 of roughly 19,800 tickers end
before the sample does. That is not a rounding error; it is a systematic upward
bias aimed squarely at the cheap, distressed names value signals love. The harness
books an explicit delisting return instead of letting those rows vanish.

**And every signal has to prove it isn't cheating.** Before anything is backtested,
the validator recomputes it on a time-truncated panel and compares:

> Recomputing a signal with the last 40% of history deleted must not change any
> earlier value — or even its missing/not-missing status.

That single check catches the entire family of look-ahead bugs. A full-sample
z-score fails it. A `.fillna()` that propagates backwards fails it. A negative shift
fails it. And notice that the NaN-status clause matters as much as the values: a
signal that quietly becomes computable earlier when it can see the future is
leaking, even if the numbers it produces look plausible.

## The part nobody builds: deciding whether the result is real

Here is the failure mode this whole project is designed around.

Suppose you generate a hundred signals, backtest them all, and report the best one.
Its Sharpe ratio is not an estimate of its quality. It's an estimate of **how many
things you tried.** Run enough random strategies against the same 280 months and
one of them will look excellent, guaranteed, with no alpha anywhere in sight.

So the leaderboard is deliberately **not** sorted by Sharpe. Three things sit on top
of it.

**Factor attribution.** Every signal's returns are regressed on market, size, value
and momentum — factors built from the same panel, so the comparison is like for
like — with Newey-West standard errors. What matters is the intercept: the return
the known premia *cannot* explain. This is brutally clarifying. The library's
`momentum_12_1` signal has a factor R² of 0.92 and an alpha t-stat of −0.10. It
isn't a discovery. It *is* the momentum factor, rediscovered, and it should be paid
for exactly once.

**A search hurdle.** Given how dispersed the Sharpes in the library are, you can
compute the Sharpe you'd expect from the *best* of N random strategies. That's the
bar luck alone clears. It is not a constant: it is recomputed on every run from the
ledger's attempt count and the spread of Sharpes across the library, so it climbs as
the search grows. Anything below it is not evidence of anything. The
[results page](../../../llm-alpha/index.qmd) carries its current value.

**Deflated Sharpe and Benjamini-Hochberg.** The deflated Sharpe is the probability a
signal is real *given* the size of the search that found it. The BH q-value controls
the false-discovery rate across the whole library at once. The denominator for both
comes from the ledger, which records every attempt — including the ones that died at
the data gate or failed to compile. Counting only survivors would understate the
search and flatter every number on the page.

This machinery has a property I've come to appreciate: **it gets harder to satisfy
the more you use it.** Every farming run adds trials, which raises the hurdle for
everything already in the library. A search large enough will push its own earlier
discoveries back below significance. That is not a bug — it is the honest accounting
finally showing up on the balance sheet.

## What it found

There is deliberately no scoreboard in this post. The campaign runs daily and the
library grows most nights, so any count printed here would be stale within a week.
Worse, a count is the wrong thing to fixate on: in this setup the number of attempts
is a *cost*, not an achievement, because every trial raises the bar for everything
already found. The [results page](../../../llm-alpha/index.qmd) regenerates itself on
every run and carries the current figures, hurdle included.

What is worth writing down is the shapes that keep recurring, because those have been
stable since the first campaign day.

**Nothing farmed has cleared the search hurdle.** Not once, not yet. The only signal
in the library that clears it is `gross_profitability` — Novy-Marx's, published in
2013, and sitting in the library before any agent ran. Even that one is labelled a
*candidate* rather than a survivor, because clearing the hurdle and surviving
multiple-testing correction with a high deflated Sharpe are two different tests, and
it passes one of them.

**Everything else works, which is the point.** Every farmed signal compiled. Every
one passed the no-look-ahead validator. Every one arrived with a coherent economic
story attached — inventory growth gaps, stock-comp dilution, oil-beta interactions,
turn-of-year tax-loss reversals. The pipeline is not failing. The hypotheses are just
wrong, in the ordinary way that most hypotheses are wrong.

**The strongest t-statistics point the wrong way.** This one I did not expect.
Several farmed signals are comfortably significant under Benjamini-Hochberg — and
negative. `attention_spike_return_reversal` posts a t-stat of −5.3 and
`filing_staleness_information_neglect` −4.4, both with Sharpes well below zero. The
agent found real cross-sectional structure and then declared the sign backwards. It
is tempting to read that as a discovery in disguise: flip `expected_sign` and you
have a strong signal. Resist it. Choosing the sign after seeing the result is just
another trial, and it is the cheapest way there is to fool yourself. If the mechanism
argument only works once you know the answer, it was never a mechanism argument.

**The search keeps rediscovering itself.** Left alone, the idea agent converges. The
library holds a cluster of same-month seasonality variants that are recognisably one
anomaly wearing different names, and pairs like `rate_duration_mispricing` and
`hidden_rate_duration_mismatch` whose return streams are nearly identical — a novelty
score of 0.02 between them. This is worse than wasted spend. Near-duplicates
manufacture trials, trials raise the hurdle, and the library ends up penalising its
own genuine entries for the sin of being asked the same question twice.
Deduplication is not housekeeping here; it is part of the statistics.

I want to be precise about what this does and doesn't show. It is a fixed dataset, a
fixed universe, and one family of ideas. It is not proof that the approach can't
work. But it is a real result, and it lines up with the thing quantitative
researchers already know and outsiders consistently underestimate: **plausible is
cheap.** The hard part of finding alpha was never generating hypotheses. A language
model generates a dozen excellent-sounding ones for under a dollar. The hard part is
that almost all hypotheses are wrong, and the only way to know which is to test them
in a way that can tell you no.

One entry is still worth watching. `market_breadth_high_ratio_timing` posts a Sharpe
of just 0.12 — nothing — but an alpha t-stat of **2.64**. Real explanatory power the
factor model misses, wrapped in a construction too weak to trade. That is the shape a
genuine discovery would first appear in, and it is exactly the shape a Sharpe-sorted
leaderboard would throw away.

## How you'd implement a signal

Everything above exists so this part can be short. Here is the whole contract:

```python
from __future__ import annotations
import pandas as pd
from llm_alpha.signals.base import BaseSignal


class GrossMarginTrend(BaseSignal):
    name = "gross_margin_trend"
    category = "quality"
    expected_sign = 1
    description = "Year-over-year change in gross margin: improving pricing power."

    def compute(self, panel: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
        gm = panel["grossmargin"]
        gm_prior = gm.groupby(level="ticker").shift(12)
        return gm - gm_prior
```

That's a complete, working signal. Four class attributes and one method. Walking
through what each part is doing:

**The panel** is a DataFrame indexed by `(date, ticker)` — one row per stock per
month-end, about 1.9 million of them. It carries price-derived features
(`ret_12_1`, `vol_252`, `beta_252`, `high_ratio`), daily valuation ratios (`pe`,
`pb`, `marketcap`), and point-in-time quarterly fundamentals (`revenue`, `assets`,
`gp`, `ncfo`, `grossmargin`, …) already joined as of their filing date. You never
load data yourself; it's all there.

**`compute` returns a Series indexed exactly like the panel.** Same index, one score
per row. Return `NaN` wherever the signal is undefined — the harness will simply
exclude those names from that month's cross-section. Missing data is expected and
handled; do not paper over it.

**`groupby(level="ticker").shift(12)`** is the single most important idiom, and the
one the coder agent most often gets wrong on its first attempt. It means "this
ticker's value twelve months ago". The `groupby` is not optional: without it, `shift`
walks off the end of one stock and into another, silently comparing Apple to
Amgen. A **negative** shift would reach into the future and the validator will
reject it.

**Guard your denominators.** The reference implementations do this everywhere:

```python
    def compute(self, panel):
        assets = panel["assets"]
        return (panel["gp"] / assets).where(assets > 0)
```

`.where(assets > 0)` yields `NaN` where the denominator is non-positive, rather
than `inf` or a sign-flipped nonsense value. A single `inf` can dominate a
cross-sectional ranking and quietly wreck a month.

**Then set `expected_sign` honestly** and don't pre-negate anything. If you believe
low values predict high returns, write the natural quantity and set `-1`.

Drop that file into `signals/library/`, and the rest is automatic: the registry
discovers it, the validator truncates the panel and checks it for look-ahead, the
harness backtests it identically to every other signal, the robustness battery
sweeps costs and sub-periods and universes, the factor model tells you whether it's
new, and the deflation layer tells you whether to believe it.

You do not get to tune any of that. Which is the point — the harness was built
before the hypotheses, precisely so it couldn't be.

## What I'd do next

The bottleneck is not the pipeline, and it is fairly clearly not the model's
imagination either. It is the **hypothesis space**, which is bounded by what the
panel contains — prices, fundamentals, a handful of macro series.

Running the same agent against the same columns another thousand times mostly
manufactures trials, and every trial raises the bar for everything already found.
Adding a genuinely new data source — short interest and borrow cost, 13F ownership
churn, analyst revisions and dispersion, options-implied skew — multiplies the space
instead of re-searching it. The other half of the same problem is the duplicate
clusters above: a correlation gate that refuses a proposal too close to something
already on the ledger would buy back hurdle for free, without needing a single new
idea.

There is a second direction, and it is about the harness rather than the ideas.
The decile long/short construction in the worked example above is deliberately
crude: every name in the top decile gets the same weight regardless of how strongly
the signal likes it, and every name outside the two extreme deciles gets nothing.
That is the right default for *judging* a signal — it is transparent, it is the
standard academic construction, and it cannot be tuned into looking good — but it
is not how anyone would actually hold the thing.

So two variants are on the list. **Position sizing**: weight by signal strength or
by inverse volatility instead of equally, so that conviction and risk both show up
in the book rather than being flattened away. And a **long-only version**, because
the short leg is where the borrow costs, the crowding and the delisting
assumptions do their real damage, and because most of the capital that would ever
run something like this cannot short at all. Both change the answer, and neither
is guaranteed to change it upwards — a signal whose spread lives entirely in the
short leg looks very different once you take the short leg away. That is precisely
what makes it worth measuring.

That's the next move: fewer, better-fed guesses rather than more of the same. The
campaign keeps running daily, and [the results page](../../../llm-alpha/index.qmd)
regenerates itself on every run, hurdle and all.
